A1.justification: Despite the changed title, both PDFs describe the same CQF research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–F support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original model-training experiments, benchmark evaluations, classifier-bias analyses, and data-conditioning experiments, including appendix results.

after.justification: v3 retains these original empirical results and adds a recursive-filtering comparison and LQ-set loss curves.

M1.justification: Section 6 adds a recursive CQF construction: a first 20% selection becomes the HQ reference for a second 1% selection. This is a limited procedural extension; the underlying embeddings, logistic-regression classifier, thresholding rule, and model architectures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The underlying RedPajama-V2 corpus, HQ sources, downstream benchmarks, and Perm/CQF tasks are retained. The new large-HQ comparison constructs filtered subsets of existing data, changing the experimental procedure rather than introducing another domain or task.

E2.justification: v3 Section 6 adds direct pretraining on the constructed, sufficiently large HQ set as a control against recursive CQF. The CRISP comparison and existing full-HQ versus top-decile fine-tuning comparisons remain unchanged. No separate data-augmentation algorithm is evaluated.

E3.justification: The new comparison uses successive 20% and 1% selections and states that both models have identical training conditions. Figure 2 also adds evaluation loss on the LQ set. Existing model configurations and training budgets in Table 2 are unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 6 adds a controlled test of whether filtering can help when the HQ set is already sufficiently large. Figure 2 adds an analysis of the loss incurred on the LQ distribution as filtering increases. Existing compute sweeps, length-bias tests, and appendix analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix C still reports averages over three runs with the same plotted uncertainty bands. Appendix E retains its standard-deviation-based discussion of graph edges. No new run-count disclosure, confidence interval, or statistical testing procedure accompanies the added comparison.

E6.justification: v3 Figure 8 newly reports 50.1% accuracy for direct training on the constructed HQ set versus 53.8% after recursive CQF under stated matched conditions. Figure 2 adds LQ-loss curves showing increasing loss with stronger filtering. The corresponding earlier benchmark, HQ-loss, scaling, and appendix results are retained.

T1.justification: The Bayes-optimal classifier argument, KL decomposition, HQ reweighting identity, data-conditioning definition, and scaling-law formula are unchanged. Moving the weight expression outside Equation 4.1 and renumbering the data-conditioning equations do not change their mathematics.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion add CQF outperforming direct training on a sufficiently large HQ set as a principal contribution. They also elevate the existing scaling analysis into a stronger claim that data-conditioning can be reliably estimated with small-scale proxies for practical dataset evaluation.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations of CQF as a distribution-shaping alternative to HQ augmentation and of data-conditioning as a selection principle. Its new Recommendations section emphasizes HQ supervision, corpus coverage, and limited HQ diversity. Existing discussions of classifier bias and task-dependent applicability remain.

D1.justification: Section 6 specifies OpenOrca as the initial reference and the 20%/1% filtering settings for the new experiment. Table 1 removes its source-description column, reducing explicit dataset provenance. Appendix F's architecture and optimization settings remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The cited works and Related Work discussion are essentially unchanged. However, Section 6 newly positions CQF as a practical alternative to costly HQ collection or synthetic augmentation, extending its positioning beyond the existing comparison with distribution-matching methods.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, research questions, and conclusion substantially reframe the narrative around practical data selection. The former discussion becomes Section 7 with a separate proxy-model subsection; Recommendations and an Impact Statement are added, and the contents page is removed.

P2.justification: Figure 2 expands from two rows to three, and Figure 8 adds the recursive-filtering diagram and results. The log-score panel from v1 Figure 4 moves to appendix Figure 12, while its PCA panel remains in the main text. Table 1 loses a column; other displays are largely retained and repositioned.

improvement.justification: The added large-HQ control and LQ-loss curves modestly strengthen the empirical analysis. The gain is limited: the new control uses an HQ set constructed by CQF and does not directly compare augmentation methods, while the stronger proxy-reliability claim still rests on the existing Perm scaling-law extrapolations. These qualifications limit the support for v3's broader practical recommendations.
